title: More useful after death
hook: dying, Dominic promised his brothers he'd help them more from heaven

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fra Angelico's cells: a quiet fresco in every friar's room. Your line was a painting in each cell.

Bologna, a friary, a hot summer. The founder is dying. Dominic, who by tradition walked the roads barefoot, and once talked all night with an innkeeper, lies on the floor, by tradition on sackcloth, too weak to rise. Around him his brothers are crying. They are young, the order is young, and they don't know how they'll manage without him. What do you say to people who are about to lose you? Dominic's answer was about the future, and it sounds almost cheeky.
screen: `BOLOGNA. THE FOUNDER IS DYING.` → `HIS BROTHERS ARE WEEPING.` → `LAST WORDS ABOUT THE FUTURE.`

segments.voice: An early life of Dominic, written by Jordan of Saxony, who led the order after him, tells it this way. Dominic saw his brothers weeping and told them not to. He would be more useful to them after his death, he said, than he had been in life. Not: I'll always be in your hearts. Not: carry on my work. But: I'm not leaving the job. I'm changing posts. Back on day ninety-six you met the cloud of witnesses; this is where it leads. The promise rests on a Catholic belief called the communion of saints. Catholics hold that the Church is one family across death: the living on earth, the dead being made ready, and the saints with God. And family members pray for one another. So asking a saint for help is, for Catholics, like asking a friend to pray for you, only the friend is now close to God. Hebrews, in the Douay-Rheims, pictures believers running their race "having so great a cloud of witnesses over our head." Christians don't all read this the same way. Catholic and Orthodox tradition asks the saints to pray. Some Protestant churches teach that prayer should go to God alone, and they honor the saints as examples rather than asking their help. Dominicans took Dominic at his word. Their tradition sings a short Latin antiphon to him that begins O spem miram, O wonderful hope, recalling this promise. A goodbye that turned into a job description.
screen: `DON'T WEEP. I'LL BE MORE USEFUL THEN.` · `ONE FAMILY ACROSS DEATH.` · `CHURCHES READ IT DIFFERENTLY.` · `O SPEM MIRAM: O WONDERFUL HOPE.` · then, large: `SO GREAT A CLOUD OF WITNESSES.`

segments.voice: If you pray to the saints, choose one, Dominic or a saint you love, and ask them plainly to pray for one thing you're carrying today. If that isn't your practice, bring to mind someone who has died who helped you, and notice where their help is still at work in you: a phrase you still use. If a loss is heavy right now, you don't have to carry it alone; in the US, 988 answers day and night, or reach local emergency help.
More useful after death. Dominic's last promise to his weeping brothers: he wasn't leaving them, he was changing posts. Today's word.
Your line: more useful then. In his promise, the young brothers weren't left on their own. Day one thousand two hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics ask the saints to pray for them, in private prayer and in the Church's litanies; Dominicans traditionally sing the antiphon O Spem Miram to Saint Dominic.

chat.says: Why would Dominic tell his crying brothers he'd be more useful after he died?
options: Catholics see the Church as one family across death; he meant he'd keep praying for them.
He meant his writings would be read more once he was gone, and would fund the order.
He meant the young brothers would finally have to lead themselves, with him out of the way.

notes: Claims rule: no date of death. 'A hot summer' (August) and 'by tradition on sackcloth' / lying on the floor: confirm against Jordan of Saxony's Libellus.
The promise is paraphrased from Jordan of Saxony (no public-domain translation quoted). Confirm wording 'more useful to them after his death than in life'.
'The earliest life of Dominic' (Jordan's Libellus): a 'first/earliest' claim taken from standard Dominican historiography; confirm or soften to 'an early life'.
Communion of saints described as living, the dead being purified, and the saints in heaven; confirm phrasing 'the dead being made ready'.
Fair description of differences: Catholic and Orthodox ask saints' intercession; some Protestant churches teach prayer to God alone and honor saints as examples. Confirm.
O Spem Miram: confirm the opening words and that it recalls the deathbed promise; 'traditionally sung' in howItsDone.
